Merged in PR #31. Pool 192.168.4.224-253 (30 addresses), scope confirmed
against the router by hand 2026-08-14.

Acceptance verified on the cluster:
  ipaddresspool/lab-pool live, autoAssign true, ['192.168.4.224-192.168.4.253']
  l2advertisement/lab-l2 bound to lab-pool
  openshift-storage/iam     -> 192.168.4.224
  openshift-storage/vectors -> 192.168.4.225
  openshift-storage/s3      -> 192.168.4.226
  openshift-storage/sts     -> 192.168.4.227

Reachability confirmed from ctrl-1: ARP resolves for all four, TCP to
192.168.4.226:443 is OPEN. ICMP to the VIPs does NOT answer - that is expected,
a LoadBalancer VIP forwards only its declared service ports, so ping is the
wrong test and its failure is not a fault. The four addresses resolved to three
distinct MACs, so MetalLB elected different speaker nodes per address rather
than concentrating them.

Range recorded in the manifest comment along with the reasoning: written as a
range rather than 192.168.4.224/27 because that CIDR spans .224-.255 and would
include the broadcast address, and kept inside 192.168.4.0/24 because
L2Advertisement answers ARP on the nodes' own broadcast domain.

Corrected a stale premise while doing this: the previous comment assumed node
addresses topped out at .142, but cnv-2 is at .182. DHCP leases drift on
renewal, so the range is justified against the router scope rather than against
observed node addresses.

Consequence accepted deliberately: autoAssign true means the four NooBaa
Services became LAN-reachable on merge. RGW already serves S3 over the Ingress
VIP, so that may be redundant exposure - autoAssign false plus
metallb.universe.tf/address-pool per Service is the documented alternative.

Fixed by Dale on the cluster and reported upstream to Red Hat.

Verified 2026-08-14 after the fix:
  allowed ports in openshift-apiserver policies: 8443, 17698  (was 8443 only)
  up{job='check-endpoints'} = 1 on all three targets
  TargetDown for check-endpoints no longer firing

Root cause as diagnosed: the namespace carried a default-deny NetworkPolicy plus
allow-apiserver permitting only TCP/8443, while the shipped ServiceMonitor
openshift-apiserver-operator-check-endpoints scrapes 17698. The i/o timeout
rather than connection refused was the tell - packets dropped by policy, not a
closed port. Confirmed pre-existing, not caused by any work in this repo:
max_over_time(up[7d]) was 0 on all three targets, and the alert's apparent onset
was an artifact of prometheus-k8s restarting.

NOTE: allow-apiserver is owned by cluster-openshift-apiserver-operator per its
managedFields, so verify after the next operator reconcile or cluster upgrade
that the added port survives. If it is reverted, that strengthens the upstream
report rather than being a new problem.

The Red Hat bug reference is not recorded here - add the link to this issue if
you want it tracked alongside the diagnosis.

THE THUMBPRINT IS NOT USED AT ALL, which resolves the placement decision recorded
here by making it moot. Testing first - as this issue instructed - showed MTV does
not require it when a valid CA is supplied and insecureSkipVerify is false. That
is the better outcome: a thumbprint pins the LEAF certificate (expires
2028-05-11) while the CA runs to 2036-05-06, so storing one would have planted a
migration-breaking expiry two years early for no security gain.

insecureSkipVerify is explicitly "false" rather than omitted, since the
certificate is ignored entirely when true and cacert would become decorative.

WHAT SHIPPED, verified on the cluster:
  vsphere-lab in open-cluster-management, SecretSynced, 21 keys, both
  cluster.open-cluster-management.io labels including the empty-valued one

WHAT WAS ESTABLISHED, which is the durable part:

1. SOURCE RULE. If the cluster already holds an authoritative copy, read it from
   the cluster; 1Password is for credentials with no in-cluster source. The pull
   secret therefore comes from openshift-config/pull-secret rather than a second
   copy in a vault that could drift.

2. TWO STORES IN ONE SECRET. spec.data[].sourceRef.storeRef mixes stores per
   entry - pullSecret via the kubernetes provider, everything else via
   1password-sdk. Proven end to end before building: the assembled pullSecret
   hashed identically to openshift-config/pull-secret.

3. TOPOLOGY IN GIT, CREDENTIALS IN A STORE. vCenter hostname, datacenter,
   cluster, datastore and baseDomain are facts, not secrets, so a reviewer can
   see what a credential targets while holding nothing sensitive.

4. THE LABELS ARE THE POINT. An ACM Credential is an ordinary Opaque Secret; the
   two labels are what make the console offer it. Wrong labels produce a Secret
   that exists and is silently never offered, so the acceptance test is the
   console listing.

5. The SSH key already existed as the 1Password 'acm' item and needed no
   manipulation - ESO reads SSHKEY-typed fields, and field labels containing
   spaces work in remoteRef.

Downstream reuse already happened: MTV's vSphere provider reads the same
1Password vcenter item under different key names (MTV 'user' vs ACM 'username'),
which is what the ESO renaming makes possible.

THE DUPLICATE OPERATORGROUP ACTUALLY HAPPENED. The console-generated
openshift-cluster-observability-operator-skb2n (created 03:13:49Z, generateName,
not ArgoCD-managed) SURVIVED the hand uninstall, so when ArgoCD created
cluster-observability-operatorgroup at 04:00:51Z the namespace had two. OLM then
refused to resolve anything in it: no CSV appeared and hub-olm-cluster-observability
sat Synced/Progressing indefinitely, with nothing reporting an error.

Fixed by deleting the stale non-ArgoCD OperatorGroup. The CSV appeared within 75
seconds and reached Succeeded at 150 seconds. Exactly the remediation written into
manifests/config/cluster-observability/README.md before it was needed.

LESSON FOR NEXT TIME: uninstalling an operator through the console does not
necessarily remove the OperatorGroup it generated. Check 'oc get operatorgroup -n
<ns>' returns exactly one before assuming a clean slate.

THE PREMISE OF THIS ISSUE WAS PARTLY WRONG AND THE INVESTIGATION CORRECTED IT.
The right-sizing fields were assumed to be an untracked hand change. Field
ownership showed otherwise:

  analytics.*RightSizingRecommendation   mco-operator   2026-08-13T23:14:02Z (install)
  metrics.default, metrics.ui            kubectl-edit   2026-08-17T17:58:35Z

So the analytics fields are OPERATOR DEFAULTS set at install, three days before
the metrics fields were patched by hand. Dale suspected the OpenShift
Virtualization settings dialog had enabled them; it had not. Only metrics was
ever a decision, so only metrics is declared - restating operator defaults would
pin a value the operator chose and silently override a future ACM release that
changed it, which clusters/hub/config.yaml already argues against.

DECLARING A VALUE ANOTHER MANAGER OWNS TURNED OUT TO BE SAFE. kubectl-edit owned
spec.capabilities, yet a server-side dry-run as argocd-controller succeeded with
no conflict: SSA makes a second manager a CO-OWNER when the value matches and
only conflicts when it differs. That is the opposite outcome to the image
registry Config, where values differed and ServerSideApply had to be disabled -
both cases are now documented side by side in the component READMEs.

STILL UNRESOLVED, and deliberately left open rather than papered over: the addon
reports platformNamespaceRightSizing=disabled and
platformVirtualizationRightSizing=disabled despite those CR fields being true,
and the grafana-dashboard-acm-right-sizing-* ConfigMaps were created three
seconds after the MCO itself - days before the fields were set - so they ship by
default and are not evidence the feature works. If right-sizing recommendations
are actually wanted, that needs its own investigation.
